title: Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention
finding: In two experiments, students studied prose passages and either restudied or completed one or three immediate free-recall tests without feedback. Restudy produced better recall on a final test after 5 minutes, but prior testing produced better retention after 2 days or 1 week. Immediate fluency and confidence therefore need not track delayed retention.
product_policy: Include low-stakes retrieval opportunities and later reviews. Distinguish practice performance from delayed retention. Offering corrective feedback is a separate design choice, not an intervention directly established by this paper's no-feedback comparison. Do not advertise a numerical learning gain for this app from this study.
scope: Controlled experiments with students, prose materials, free recall, and final tests at specified delays.
limitations: Does not directly establish algebra problem-solving transfer, an optimal scheduler, a universal target error rate, or desktop-app efficacy.
The original abstract was verified; full-paper PDF retrieval failed certificate/access checks. No sample-size or effect-size claim is made from unavailable full text.

title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis
finding: The original meta-analysis identified 839 assessments from 317 experiments in 184 articles. Interstudy interval and retention interval jointly affected final recall: the spacing associated with maximal retention increased as the intended retention interval increased. Longer spacing is not an unconditional 'more is always better' rule.
product_policy: Distribute practice over time, specify the retention horizon, and test scheduling choices against later recall and transfer. Do not present one universal interval schedule or a fixed struggle percentage as established by this review.
scope: Quantitative synthesis specifically of verbal recall tasks; spacing, lag, and temporal moderators.
limitations: Task and timing heterogeneity constrain direct extrapolation to mathematical reasoning or every learner population.
The study does not validate HLR, BKT, a 70% correctness threshold, or this product's efficacy.

title: A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning
finding: Half-life regression models recall as p = 2^(-elapsed_time/half_life), with trainable half-life features. Evaluation used 12.9 million Duolingo instances, the first 90% for training and remaining 10% for testing. HLR achieved recall-rate MAE 0.128 and at least 45% lower MAE than the Leitner baseline. Leitner nevertheless had the highest AUC among the compared algorithms. Prediction error reduction is not a learning-gain percentage.
product_policy: Treat HLR as a candidate forgetting model. Fit and calibrate it on authorized, domain-appropriate histories; compare it with simple spacing baselines using chronological held-out data. Keep next-response prediction, ranking, delayed retention, and transfer as different evaluation targets. Use conservative cold-start behavior rather than invented personalized half-lives.
scope: Second-language word/lexeme recall in Duolingo; historical prediction and production student-model use.
limitations: Language-learning parameters are not automatically valid for algebra knowledge components.
Sparse lexeme features overfit and frustrated some users; removing them addressed cold-start and experience problems.
Predictive fit does not establish a causal improvement in delayed transfer or durable conceptual mastery.

title: Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics
finding: Across 225 studies of undergraduate STEM classrooms, active learning was associated with a mean examination/concept-inventory improvement of 0.47 standard deviations in 158 studies. In 67 failure-rate studies, traditional lecturing had a failure odds ratio of 1.95, approximately a risk ratio of 1.5. These are different quantities. Reported average failure rates were 33.8% under lecture and 21.8% under active learning.
product_policy: Prefer meaningful solving, explaining, retrieval, and feedback over passive consumption alone. Do not equate clicking with active learning or promise the meta-analysis effect size for a self-study desktop app. Assess the actual intervention rather than its label.
scope: In-class undergraduate STEM instructional designs, examinations, concept inventories, and course failure; not a study of desktop software or solitary AI tutoring.
limitations: Active-learning formats and intensity varied widely; the review could not estimate an optimal intensity/type from available data.
Many studies were quasi-experimental; the failure-rate evidence lacked randomized designs.
Volunteer instructors and context may affect generalization; it is not known that universal implementation would preserve the same effect size.
The approximate 6% examination-score description is not a universal app gain.

title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
year_note: Nominal journal issue is 2008, volume 9(3), 105-119. The accessible author PDF bears 2009 copyright and the publisher/search metadata also reports 2009 online publication; retain this distinction rather than treating the DOI's year as the issue year.
finding: The review found virtually no evidence for the interaction pattern needed to validate instructional 'meshing' with diagnosed learning styles, and no adequate evidence base to justify routine learning-style assessments. A credible test requires grouping by assessed style, random assignment to instructional methods, the same outcome assessment, and a style-by-method interaction in which the best method differs by style.

scope: Evidence review of learning-style-based instructional matching, not all personalization or all accessibility accommodations.
limitations: Lack of adequate meshing validation is not proof that all individual differences or every possible personalization are ineffective.
The authors explicitly caution that many possible versions had not been tested with sound methods.
The review is historical; it is not an exhaustive review of all later literature.

title: Knowledge tracing: Modeling the acquisition of procedural knowledge
year_note: Requested and Springer-indexed citation is 1994. APA lists 1994-1995. The original scanned article says 1995, received 1 December 1994 and final form 13 March 1995; it is commonly cited as 1995. This record preserves the discrepancy explicitly.
finding: The ACT Programming Tutor estimated the probability that each production rule was learned and individualized practice from those estimates. Original BKT uses learned/unlearned states, an initial-learning probability, learning-transition probability, guess probability, and slip probability. It explicitly assumes no learned-to-unlearned transition. Successive empirical refinements included rule difficulty and individual differences; the article reports useful prediction of test performance.
product_policy: Use BKT as an interpretable candidate model for carefully defined knowledge components, not as a direct measurement of the mind. Expose estimates as uncertain. Validate skill tags, parameters, and out-of-tutor predictions. For long-term use, do not silently assume no forgetting: evaluate a forgetting extension or separate retention model. Distinguish latent learned-state probability from next-answer correctness.
scope: Procedural programming knowledge in ACT tutoring, including Lisp and related programming modules; a sequence of modeling studies, not a universal adaptive-app trial.
limitations: Two-state representation, component independence, single-action attribution, parameter identifiability, and no-forgetting assumptions constrain interpretation.
An answer may be correct by guessing or incorrect through a slip; neither establishes mastery or nonmastery deterministically.
A high mastery probability or a tutor's chosen criterion is not a universal optimal training accuracy and does not guarantee delayed transfer.
OCR introduces potential transcription errors; no new numeric effect-size claim is made from the scan.

title: Performance Factors Analysis – A New Alternative to Knowledge Tracing
finding: PFA models next-performance probability through logistic regression with knowledge-component difficulty and separate coefficients for prior successes and failures. It supports combining multiple components. Comparisons used fractions, algebra, geometry, and physics tutor datasets. PFA was somewhat superior to the particular KT implementations on reported fit statistics and reacted less aggressively to a single failure; full LFA was marginally better on several comparisons with subject effects.
product_policy: Compare PFA and BKT against simple baselines on authorized, correctly tagged data. Use only prior observations when constructing success/failure counts. Report chronological held-out log loss, Brier score, calibration, and discrimination, including new-user and new-item tests. Do not infer that better predictive fit causes better learning or that PFA is always superior.
scope: Original educational data-mining/model comparison using four specific tutor datasets with supplied knowledge-component labels.
limitations: Results depend on dataset labels, parameter constraints, KT fitting procedures, and treatment of multi-component responses.
The reported KT comparison is not an app-specific randomized outcome experiment; fit statistics are not durable mastery or transfer effects.
The basic success/failure-count model does not itself model elapsed-time forgetting or fully distinguish response order.
A chronological validation protocol is a product requirement proposed here, not a claim that the paper used that exact protocol.

title: The Eighty Five Percent Rule for optimal learning — boundary on generalization
finding: This paper derives an approximately 15.87% optimal training error rate for a class of stochastic-gradient-descent learning algorithms in binary classification and demonstrates it with artificial and biologically plausible neural networks. title: Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures
finding: Two experiments with 80 students learning a 21-minute statistics video associated interpolated memory tests with reduced reported mind wandering, more note taking, and improved learning of the lecture's final segment. The original published paper spells the second author's surname Khan; an institutional listing uses Kahn.
product_policy: Label window focus, mouse/keyboard events, elapsed time, video playback, and inactivity as activity proxies, not cognitive attention measurements. Reading, thinking, accessibility tools, interruptions, and background activity can break any assumed mapping. Optional self-report probes can supplement assessment but do not make continuous attention observable. Do not issue attention diagnoses or punitive scores.
scope: Small controlled experiments on a short online lecture, self-reported mind wandering, notes, and immediate learning outcomes.
limitations: The study did not validate desktop clickstream attention inference, a continuous attention score, or camera-based attention surveillance.
Thought probes and retrospective self-reports have measurement limits and are not cognitive ground truth.
Immediate lecture performance does not establish delayed transfer or general app efficacy.

finding: Quantitative and qualitative analysis of conversations in twelve sixth-grade triads linked problem-solving outcomes to proposal characteristics, partner responsiveness, and uptake of correct ideas. title: Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text
finding: The original study evaluated 12 publicly available AI-text detection tools and two commercial systems. It concluded that the evaluated tools were neither accurate nor reliable for distinguishing the tested human and generated documents; transformations such as obfuscation worsened performance. These findings concern the tested 2023 tools, not every future system.
product_policy: Treat anti-AI indicators as uncertain review cues, never proof of AI use or cheating. Timing, paste events, fast responses, inactivity, or writing-style changes cannot by themselves establish authorship or AI use. Do not auto-accuse, punish, or deny learning access. Account for expertise, prepared work, network latency, assistive technology, and human variability. Prefer disclosed tool-use rules, optional process explanations, and independently assessed transfer. Provide human review and appeal where stakes exist.
scope: Specific 2023 AI-generated text detectors and document transformations; timing-only indicators were not studied.
limitations: The timing restriction is a conservative product evidentiary rule, not an empirical timing effect reported by this study.
No detector benchmark for this desktop app was performed.
False-positive and false-negative risks remain context- and base-rate-dependent; present-day detector accuracy cannot be inferred from historical results.

title: Proposed preregistered randomized within-user delayed-retention and transfer benchmark
finding: No learning-outcome experiment was run in this research-only task. The cited retrieval and spacing evidence motivates measuring delayed outcomes but does not itself validate this protocol or establish product efficacy. The following is a proposed acceptance benchmark, not a reported result.
product_policy: Preregister a randomized within-user comparison on matched, nonoverlapping skill/item-family blocks. Each consenting learner receives both adaptive and fixed evidence-informed practice with a matched time budget. Do not repeatedly switch the same learned skill between treatments and assume learning washes out. Independently assess delayed unassisted retention and novel transfer. Require app-specific human outcome evidence before efficacy marketing.
scope: A consented target-population algebra pilot followed by a sufficiently powered confirmatory study; generalization limited to sampled learners, curriculum and tested app version.
limitations: Knowledge transfer between related blocks, time/order effects, external study, motivation, nonadherence and missing delayed tests can bias a within-user estimate.
Learning is not reversible, so conventional washout on the same items is invalid; nonoverlapping matched blocks and counterbalanced order reduce but do not eliminate carryover.
An underpowered or single-user trial is exploratory and cannot justify population efficacy claims.
Any bundled treatment difference estimates the bundle, not the isolated effect of each algorithm or threshold.

benchmark_plan.population_and_consent: Recruit the intended learner population with voluntary research consent, accessibility accommodations, stated allowed outside aids, and a decline/withdrawal path without losing core learning access. Obtain any required child/guardian and institutional approvals before enrollment. Report recruitment, eligibility, baseline proficiency and app/content versions.
benchmark_plan.unit_and_randomization: Within each learner, use several expert-matched pairs of nonoverlapping knowledge-component/item-family blocks balanced on pretest proficiency and estimated difficulty. Randomly assign one member of each pair to adaptive practice and the other to a fixed evidence-informed schedule; counterbalance order and content-to-condition assignments across learners. Treat tightly linked prerequisites as a cluster to reduce cross-condition leakage. Store the allocation seed and probabilities.

arms.adaptive: A frozen, versioned scheduling/difficulty policy using only prior in-condition practice history, with bounded challenge settings and user-requested hints/stopping.
arms.control: A prespecified fixed spacing/difficulty policy with the same interface, instruction quality, feedback/hint availability, curriculum coverage opportunity and assigned practice-time budget. Use an evidence-informed comparator, not an intentionally weak or unsafe condition.

benchmark_plan.threshold_experiment: Keep any 70% correctness setting or fixed struggle/challenge percentage explicitly hypothetical. To isolate a threshold effect, compare prespecified safe target bands while holding other policy components constant; use separate randomized matched blocks or a planned factorial design with sufficient power. Define whether the target means predicted or observed first-attempt correctness and measure calibration. No band is declared universally optimal beforehand.
benchmark_plan.outcome_schedule: Before randomization obtain a brief independent pretest. Assess unassisted retention and novel transfer after a prespecified delay such as 7 days, with a second assessment such as 28 days. These are protocol choices, not universally optimal delays. Define timing anchors relative to the intervention end; keep the assigned practice window and test timing comparable, log actual exposure and last practice, and state whether additional post-window practice is allowed.
benchmark_plan.primary_outcome: Blinded score on independently authored or licensed, unseen transfer tasks at the primary delayed assessment. Tasks must require applying the trained concepts in new surface forms/contexts rather than repeating training answers. Freeze the rubric and content before the trial; ensure graders do not see allocation or telemetry. Estimate the adaptive-minus-control within-user difference with uncertainty.
secondary_outcomes: Delayed unassisted retention on independent parallel items
Assigned and actual practice time, hint use and completion
Optional frustration/workload reports and adverse experiences
Engagement as a distinct secondary behavioral measure, not mastery
benchmark_plan.test_integrity_and_carryover: Hold assessment items/rubrics out of scheduler training, prompts, feedback and model updates. Keep AI and hints unavailable in the assessment UI under disclosed, consented conditions without covert surveillance. Use explanations and unfamiliar transfer rather than claiming timing proves independence. Use parallel forms at successive tests because an earlier test is itself retrieval practice; apply that exposure consistently to both conditions and acknowledge it. Log outside study voluntarily and prespecify sensitivity analyses.
benchmark_plan.analysis: Preregister the primary estimand, smallest educationally meaningful effect, outcome hierarchy, exclusion rules, missing-data handling and stopping rule. Use a paired/mixed-effects or randomization-based analysis respecting learner and randomized skill-block clustering, baseline scores and counterbalanced order. Report raw paired differences, effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals; adjust multiplicity for confirmatory secondary claims. Analyze by assigned condition first, disclose adherence, and perform prespecified missingness/carryover sensitivity analyses. Never count repeated answers as independent participants.
benchmark_plan.sample_size: Use pilot variance, within-user correlation, cluster structure, intended meaningful effect and delayed-test attrition to justify confirmatory sample size. Do not invent a fixed participant count or assume literature effect sizes equal the app's effect.
benchmark_plan.acceptance: Before data collection define meaningful benefit and acceptable harm bounds with domain experts. An efficacy claim requires a prespecified delayed-transfer result supporting the meaningful benefit threshold with its confidence interval, no unacceptable adverse-experience tradeoff, and robustness checks; preferably replicate. Otherwise report null, negative or inconclusive results honestly, with no efficacy claim. A nonsignificant result is not proof of equivalence.
benchmark_plan.software_vs_learning: Unit/integration/security tests, model prediction benchmarks, successful packaging, visual polish and end-to-end workflow success are engineering acceptance only. They cannot establish human learning gains, cognitive attention, creativity, collaboration or AI-use detection accuracy. Record learning-outcome study status separately.

title: Research and product acceptance must be bounded, transparent and non-guaranteed
finding: The instruction to continue until 'perfect' cannot establish that perfection, universal success or zero residual risk is achievable. This file records evidence and a proposed human-outcome benchmark; it does not certify the existing application's implementation, safety, learning efficacy or complete legal compliance.

title: Algebra and Trigonometry (1e) — CC BY 4.0 as reported by OpenStax's own book API
finding: OpenStax's CMS book API (apps/cms/api/v2/pages/38/) reports the first edition of Algebra and Trigonometry with license_name 'Creative Commons Attribution License', license_version 4.0, license_url https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ — BY only, no NC, no ND. This contrasts with every current 2e edition checked the same day (Algebra 1, College Algebra 2e, Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, Elementary Algebra 2e, Intermediate Algebra 2e, Prealgebra 2e), all of which report CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The 1e is book_state 'retired' from the storefront but its webview pages are still served with server-rendered prose and citation_* metadata. The licensing-transition evidence (openstax_license_transition) confirms the move is from a CC BY mix to NC for new versions, not a revocation of the CC BY grant on the 1e.
product_policy: Text storage is cleared for THIS edition only. The fetcher (app/ingest/sources/openstax.py) re-classifies the licence from the publisher's API at every fetch and refuses to store text unless the live classification still matches this audited CC BY entry; 2e editions and unaudited slugs stay link-only. Stored sections are quoted deterministically into rendered lessons and never sent to a model, per OpenStax's own prohibition on ingesting its content into LLMs or generative-AI offerings: the quote lives in a callout block the prose-rewriting pass never reads, and agent-loop tool results are redacted by app.harness.generate.redact_textbook_quotes (verbatim text replaced with a withholding notice, citation kept).
scope: OpenStax CMS API record for book id 38 (book_uuid 13ac107a-f15f-49d2-97e8-60ab2e3b519c) and the publisher-served webview pages under /books/algebra-and-trigonometry/pages/, as served on 11 October 2026.
limitations: The 1e is retired from OpenStax's storefront; if the webview pages are withdrawn, fetches fail closed to status 'unavailable' rather than serving a cached text as current.
Third-party components inside sections (photos, embedded resources) carry their own rights; the CC BY grant is OpenStax's for its own content. Quotes are prose only.

title: OpenStax book catalogue licences as reported by the publisher's CMS API (2026-11-10 snapshot)
finding: The publisher's own CMS book listing reports 129 books. 38 report Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (BY only) -- predominantly retired first editions (Algebra and Trigonometry, Biology, Chemistry, Precalculus, the Principles of Economics set, Psychology, Introductory Statistics) plus live titles Physics, Statistics and Introduction to Intellectual Property. 80 report Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 (all current 2e editions). 11 -- the Spanish translations and one courseware shell -- report NO licence fields at all. The licence fields read here are the same ones the runtime fetcher re-reads per book at fetch time.
product_policy: Each catalogue book is registered with the rights position its own publisher data supports: CC BY books are text-eligible subject to per-fetch live re-verification against the same API (drift fails closed); NC books are link-only and withheld from a paid offering; no-licence books are refused outright with zero network requests. Section text is never sent to a model regardless of class, mirroring OpenStax's AI-ingestion notice. The snapshot (app/ingest/sources/openstax_catalogue.json) stores raw publisher fields only and is refreshed exclusively by scripts/refresh_openstax_catalogue.py.
scope: Publisher CMS listing served 2026-11-10 (129 books, fields verified in the same response shape the fetcher uses).
limitations: Licence fields are per-book publisher metadata; a book's webview or preface could carry additional third-party exceptions not visible in the listing.
The 11 no-licence books may be a CMS metadata gap rather than a rights change; they stay refused until the publisher declares a licence, which is the conservative reading.
A snapshot is a point-in-time audit; the refresh script, not this file, is how the picture stays current.
